title: When does "only a few left" work?
principle: Scarce things feel more valuable. Only claim scarcity that is true.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a phone. On 2 December 2014, the OnePlus One went on sale in India. You could buy it only on Amazon, and only with an invite. Why make a phone so hard to buy? A study about cookies gives a clue.

screens.prompt: In a 1975 study, people tasted the same cookies, from a jar with 10 cookies or a jar with 2. Which did they like more?

options.label: The cookies from the jar with 10
The cookies from the jar with 2
Both the same, as they were the same cookies

screens.why: The jar with 2. Same cookies, but fewer in the jar made them feel more special. Nothing about the cookies changed.

screens.title: Scarcity
screens.text: This is called scarcity. When something is hard to get, we want it more. In the same study, a third group's jar went from 10 cookies to 2 in front of them. They liked the cookies most of all. The OnePlus invites worked on the same feeling.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: You see it all the time: "only 2 rooms left, 30 people looking", countdown timers, "limited drop". Some are true. Many are not. In 2023, India's consumer authority banned "false urgency": saying stock or time is running out when it isn't.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A phone launch and a home bakery seem far apart, but you've seen this go wrong already. In June, posting "Only 5 cakes left!" twice made the new colony stop ordering for a while. Now Christmas plum cakes are your biggest order of the year.

screens.title: A real limit
screens.text: Plum cake fruit must soak for weeks. In November, you soaked fruit for 40 cakes, and no more. Each cake sells for ₹1,200 and costs ₹600 to make. So you can sell only 40 this Christmas. That limit is real.

screens.prompt: True or false: "Only 40 plum cakes" is fair, even if you could have soaked fruit for 80 but chose 40.

options.label: True: a limit I chose is still real
False: only limits I can't change count

screens.why: True. You chose 40, and you'll make exactly 40. The limit is real, so saying it is honest. False urgency is a limit that isn't real.

wrong.b: A batch size you choose is still a real limit, as long as you keep it. Many bakers make a set number. False urgency is a limit that isn't real at all.

screens.prompt: You must close orders in time to bake every cake before Christmas. Which post is honest?

options.label: "Only 3 left!" on every post, all month
"Order in 10 minutes, or the price goes up!"
"40 plum cakes only. Orders close 20 December."

screens.why: Exactly. The number and the date are both real, and you said them plainly. Buyers can plan, and nobody feels tricked.

wrong.a: "Only 3 left" every day for a month is false. Buyers notice, like the mother in June did. Say the real limit plainly: 40 cakes, orders close 20 December.
wrong.b: That's a fake deadline. Nothing changes in 10 minutes, and buyers who feel pushed often walk away. Say the real limit: 40 cakes, orders close 20 December.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six messages. For each one, tell me: is the limit true, or is it false urgency?

items.text: "40 cakes only", when you soaked fruit for 40
A countdown timer that starts again every day
"6 seats in my baking class", and your kitchen fits 6
"Only 2 left!" when you can bake 20 more
"Orders close 20 December", so every cake is ready for Christmas
"30 people are looking right now!", a made-up count

screens.why: A true limit has a real reason behind it: fruit, seats, time. A timer that restarts, a fake "only 2 left" or made-up viewers are false urgency, and India bans them.

screens.setup: It's 18 December. 34 of your 40 plum cakes are booked, so 6 are left. An office on your birthday-cake plan now wants 20 plum cakes. Each leaves you ₹600. Your chocolate cake leaves you ₹450.
screens.question: What do you tell the office?

options.label: "Yes to all 20." Then rush 14 more with unsoaked fruit
options.outcome: The rushed cakes taste dry. The office pays for the 6 good ones and returns the 14. They cost you ₹8,400 to make. After the 6 good cakes, you're ₹4,800 down.
options.why: Your limit was real, and ignoring it broke the product. A real limit protects quality.
options.better: Offer the 6 plum cakes, plus chocolate cakes for the rest.

options.label: "Sorry, we're sold out", and keep the 6 for others
options.outcome: The office orders elsewhere. The last 6 plum cakes sell to families by 20 December, leaving you ₹3,600.
options.why: Honest, and the limit stayed real. But you didn't offer what you could make.
options.better: Offer the 6 plum cakes, plus chocolate cakes for the rest.

options.label: "6 plum cakes left, and chocolate cakes for the rest"
options.outcome: The office takes 6 plum cakes and 14 chocolate cakes. You keep ₹3,600 plus ₹6,300: ₹9,900. The manager asks to book 30 plum cakes in October, for next Christmas.
options.why: You kept your real limit and still helped. Next year, they'll order early because they know the limit is true.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: The line one last time: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Say a real limit plainly: how many, and until when. Never fake one. False urgency is against the law in India, and buyers who catch it stop trusting you.
Scarce things feel more ___. Only claim scarcity that is ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Hard-to-get invites made the phone feel special. Your 40 real plum cakes, with a real closing date, feel special too, and nobody feels tricked.

summary: Scarcity: when something is hard to get, we want it more.
Say real limits plainly: the number, the date, and the reason.
False urgency (fake "only 2 left", restarting timers) is banned in India and kills trust.

cards.front: You can make only 40 hampers. Is "Only 40 hampers, orders close Friday" fair?
options: No, every limit is a trick
cards.back: Scarcity that is true and said plainly is fair.

cards.front: A website shows "Only 2 left!" every day for a month. What is it?
cards.back: False urgency is one of the dark patterns India banned in 2023.

cards.front: In one study, cookies from which jar were rated tastier?
cards.back: Scarce things feel more valuable, even when nothing else changes.

sources.label: OnePlus One available in India without an invite on Feb 10 (FoneArena, 2015)
Scarcity (social psychology): Worchel, Lee and Adewole's cookie jar study (1975)
